reading.rtitle: Ward Voices -- a reviewer's report on an art and health project
paras: Ward Voices is a sound work built from interviews with twelve caregivers in a public hospital, recorded over eighteen months. This is a serious project, and the rigor of the transcripts is obvious on every page. The artist must have spent a great deal of time on the ward before anybody agreed to be recorded; nobody gets testimony this candid in a single visit. The project also sits in a real gap in the literature: caregivers are usually quoted by doctors and researchers, and almost never heard as authors of their own accounts.

The limitations are real, and the application is right to name some of them. A sample of twelve cannot be representative of a hospital of four thousand staff, and the claim in section three, that the recordings show how all caregivers experience the night shift, overreaches. The evidence is anecdotal, which is appropriate for an artwork but not for a claim about everybody. Some families might have told the artist what they believed she wanted to hear, and the application does not account for the six people who refused to be recorded. Their silence may be part of the story.

The date given for the closure of the old ward cannot be right: the hospital records place it two years later, and nothing in the application corroborates the earlier date. The artist may have been relying on a single memory. None of this is fatal. The method is robust, and the central reading of the material is plausible. The final section, on what the work might change in hospital policy, is speculative, and the first phase of evaluation was inconclusive. I recommend funding, on the condition that the second phase includes a paragraph on limitations as honest as the recordings themselves.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson as a realistic reviewer's report on a funding application

reading.prompt: What is the reviewer's overall position?
choices: The project should be rejected because the evidence is anecdotal.
The project is serious and should be funded, if it names its limits more honestly.
The project proves how all caregivers experience the night shift.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: Thank you for such a careful reading of the project.
You are right: a sample of twelve cannot speak for the whole hospital.
The date must have come from a single memory, and I will check the records.
That section is speculative, and I will say so more clearly.
I will account for the six people who refused to be recorded.
The method is robust, but the conclusions need to be smaller.

listenings.text: I sit on a panel that funds projects between the arts and medicine, and the first thing I read in any application is not the idea. It is the paragraph on limitations. If it is missing, the applicant cannot have thought very hard about the work, or they must be hoping we will not notice. If it is there and it is honest, I relax. The best one I read this year said, more or less: we interviewed twelve families, so this cannot be a claim about the whole city; some of them might have told us what they thought we wanted to hear; and we do not yet know whether the effect lasts beyond six months. Three sentences, three modals, and I trusted everything else in that application more because of them. Admitting what you do not know is not weakness on a panel. It is the clearest sign of rigor we have.

People outside research imagine that a review is a verdict. It is closer to a conversation with somebody who has read your work more carefully than anybody else will. When a reviewer writes that a claim must be overstated, the useful response is not to defend it. It is to ask what evidence would corroborate it, and whether you have that evidence. Sometimes you do, and you simply forgot to include it. Sometimes you do not, and the claim has to become smaller and more honest. In my field, the humanities side of medicine, most of our evidence is anecdotal by design. That is not a flaw we hide. It is a limitation we name, and naming it is what allows the stories to be taken seriously. A report that sounds certain about everything is the one I would trust least.
